title: In-Situ Coupling of Tensor Basis Neural Networks for Turbulence Modeling in OpenFOAM: A Critical Verification, Validation, and Reproducibility Study
description:
Linear eddy viscosity models based on the Boussinesq hypothesis remain the workhorse of industrial Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD). However, they fundamentally fail to predict turbulence-driven secondary flows of Prandtl's second kind due to their enforced alignment between the Reynolds stress anisotropy tensor and the mean strain rate tensor. Data-driven turbulence closures utilizing Tensor Basis Neural Networks (TBNN; Ling et al., J. Fluid Mech., 2016) provide a mathematically rigorous, frame-invariant methodology to represent Reynolds stress anisotropy by projecting onto Pope's ten symmetric integrity basis tensors.

In this work, we present an in-situ coupled CFD solver, tbnnFoam, implemented within OpenFOAM 2606. The solver features a dual-runtime inference architecture: an embedded LibTorch C++ engine and a zero-dependency standalone C++ matrix evaluator incorporating an analytical Cardano cubic eigensolver that enforces physical realizability on the Lumley triangle in \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) operations. Cross-engine numerical parity across PyTorch, TorchScript, and the standalone C++ matrix evaluator is verified within an absolute tolerance of 10-5 across synthetic test cases spanning shear, rotational, and complex 3D strain states, with the standalone C++ comparison executed when the OpenFOAM environment and compiled test binary are present. Beyond evaluator parity, the momentum-equation coupling itself is verified by an assembled-matrix test: in the Boussinesq limit the coupled equation reduces exactly to the baseline linear model (maximum relative deviation 3.6 × 10-17).

We validate the coupled solver on developing turbulent flow in a square duct at bulk Reynolds number Reb ≈ 4410 (Reτ = 150) against high-fidelity Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS; Pirozzoli et al., J. Fluid Mech., 2018). An independent algorithmic vortex detector employing connected-component labeling on non-dimensional axial vorticity confirms that tbnnFoam structurally recovers the secondary-flow mechanism by identifying all eight counter-rotating secondary recirculation cells where the standard linear k–ω SST closure tested here fails to reproduce the secondary-flow topology (detecting zero vortex cores).

The outcome is a partial validation: while secondary circulation topology is recovered, vortex core localization exhibits notable offset (0.567 h error on the coarse mesh and 0.447 h on the refined mesh against the raw-field-verified DNS reference (0.577, 0.847)), and peak secondary speed exhibits strong discretization sensitivity, decreasing from 7.99% to 2.62% under 4× cross-stream grid refinement (relative to the raw-field DNS peak of 1.93%). We analyze the sources of these discrepancies, including the empirical ω surrogate whose invariants scale as τ2 through τ4, first-order upwinding, wall-target degeneracy, and the developing-flow versus periodic-DNS mismatch, and quantify distribution shift between training and live states (median k-NN distance 0.21 σ). All solver sources, evaluation scripts, raw DNS benchmark data, and an automated 21-test verification suite are openly distributed under the MIT license.
